subject: science
passage: In the rainy hills of Meghalaya, in northeastern India, Khasi villagers have long built bridges by guiding the aerial roots of rubber fig trees across streams until the roots take hold on the far bank. Over decades, such bridges become strong enough to carry many people at once. Engineer Banshan Lyngdoh proposes that this growing strength comes mainly from the way the roots fuse together wherever they cross, forming a connected network, rather than simply from each root growing thicker with age.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Lyngdoh's proposal?

choices.A: Among bridges with roots of similar thickness, those with more fused junctions held heavier loads.
choices.B: The rubber fig trees used for the bridges grow especially well in Meghalaya's heavy seasonal rains.
choices.C: Bridges that had been growing for many decades held heavier loads than younger bridges did.
choices.D: Bridges with thicker roots held heavier loads no matter how many of their junctions had fused.

explanation.why: Lyngdoh names two things that happen as a bridge ages: roots fuse and roots thicken. He credits the fusing. Support must therefore hold thickness constant and show that more fusion still means more strength.
explanation.A: Correct. With thickness held equal, the extra strength of bridges with more junctions can come only from fusion, as Lyngdoh proposes.
explanation.B: Incorrect. How well the trees grow in the rain does not show which feature of the roots makes the bridges strong.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Older bridges have both thicker roots and more junctions, so their greater strength does not show which feature is responsible.
explanation.D: Incorrect. If thickness alone predicted strength, fusion would not matter much; this weakens Lyngdoh's proposal.
